The core contribution of RADAR lies in its ability to address the limitations of current neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) models, which often assume symmetric Euclidean distances, thereby restricting their applicability in real-world scenarios where routing is influenced by factors like one-way streets and traffic congestion. RADAR tackles the challenge of asymmetric VRPs through two primary mechanisms: an SVD-based initialization and Sinkhorn normalization within the attention mechanism. The SVD-based initialization aims to capture static asymmetries by creating compact embeddings that encode each node's role as a source and destination, preserving global directionality. Specifically, the distance matrix is decomposed using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and the resulting components are used to initialize node embeddings. This approach seeks to address the limitations of previous attempts at encoding static asymmetry, which often lose global structure and underperform. The Sinkhorn normalization, on the other hand, addresses dynamic asymmetries by imposing joint row and column distance awareness in the attention weights. This ensures balanced bidirectional flows, allowing the attention score to capture interactions that depend not only on each node's own neighborhood but also on the neighborhood structure of its counterparts. The authors evaluate RADAR on a diverse set of 17 synthetic and 3 real-world VRP variants, demonstrating its superior performance and robust generalization compared to existing methods. The empirical results consistently show that RADAR outperforms strong baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, highlighting its practical significance in solving asymmetric VRPs. Overall, the paper makes a valuable contribution to the field of neural combinatorial optimization by addressing a critical gap in the handling of asymmetric VRPs.
